extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, judges, and law students (those drafting or litigating patent specifications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for drafting the specification portion of a patent: what must be disclosed, how claims and descriptions should be framed, and how courts construe sufficiency, clarity, and scope. Focuses on enablement, best mode, claim scope, and avoidance of abstract claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of most advantageous mode and conducive circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to disclose the most advantageous mode known to him; and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If useless or unnecessary matters are introduced into the specification as if essential, the patent may be declared void because such material may be presumed to have been inserted to overload and cloud the description and conceal the real invention. (Discussed with reference to English authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — specification must enable a skilled mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be described with such accuracy as will enable a competent/skilful mechanic to put the invention in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification may be less perfect than desirable but still sufficient if a skilful mechanic can attain the end without new inventive power or experiments (cf. Carver v. The Braintree Manufacturing Company). The key question: has the patentee communicated to the public the manner of carrying his invention into effect and given all the knowledge he had?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing useless ingredients or steps
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification inserts ingredients or steps which are unnecessary to produce the claimed effect, and the patentee never used them, the patent may be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Arkwright (extra parts introduced but not necessary); Turner's patent where extra ingredients were listed that did not produce the desired effect — insertion of unnecessary details can render the patent void because it fails to put the public in possession of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden when patentee improves after issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee employs an improved mode of working different from the specification, he may bear the burden of showing the improvement was made after issuing of the patent; otherwise it may be presumed he withheld the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrastingly, if a patentee claims as his invention a part that turns out useless but did not describe it as essential, that may not vitiate the patent. The facts determine whether a later improvement undermines the specification's sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be full and explicit to permit infringement to be determined
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should be full and explicit enough to prevent the public from infringing the patentee's right; infringement will not have taken place unless the invention can be practised completely by following the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent does not fully describe everything essential to making/doing the thing patented, a later party who makes a complete device by adding withheld information may not infringe. A patent should put the public in possession of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding of processes limits infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee withholds invention of processes from the public, subsequent independent inventions of those processes will not be infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is that a 'fresh invention' of processes which the patentee has withheld cannot be an infringement because the public was not put in possession of those processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguity and misuse of terms — clarity of terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity produced by misuse of terms that renders the specification unintelligible is as fatal as any other defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using 'sea-salt, or sal-gem, or fossil-salt' when only 'sal-gem' could be used misleads and creates unnecessary experiments. Similarly, inventing nonexistent trade terms (e.g., 'finest and purest chemical white-lead' when no such substance exists) is defective. Minor word mistakes may be immaterial if explained elsewhere in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When improvement is the invention, confine claim to the improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of an improvement, when the improvement is the real subject-matter of the patent, should clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a machine substantially existed before and the patentee makes an improvement, the patent should not comprehend the whole machine in its improved state but should be confined to the improvement, even if the addition produces the same effects better or creates new combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite prior use when claiming an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is an improvement but nothing is said of previous use, the patent may be construed as a claim of an entire and original discovery; accordingly there is a necessity for reciting what had formerly been done and describing the different mode as the improvement claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to qualify an improvement with a recital of prior art or prior use may render the claim broader than intended and risk invalidity (illustrated by Brooks v. Bicknell and cases concerning lime applied to iron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail required for improvements to known machines
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing the improvement of a machine in use and well known, it is not necessary to state in detail the structure of the entire and improved machine; it is sufficient to describe the parts of which the improvement consists and the effects it produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requisition exists to ensure fullness and clearness, but where prior art machine is known, only the improvement's components and effects must be shown rather than the whole machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement to explain principle and several modes
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of any machine, the patentee shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle, and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 'principle' is meant the peculiar structure and mode of operation; the statute presumes the patentee should point out all modes of applying the principle which he claims to cover, whether preferred or mere formal variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the several modes of application and indicate variations claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is to state not only the peculiar device he deems best, but also all the other modes of producing the same effect which he means to claim as substantially applications of the same principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He need not enter into minute descriptions of every variation; it is sufficient to indicate what variations of application of the principle he claims beyond his preferred mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming an abstract principle or mere function
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot appropriate a mere abstract principle, law of nature, or function by stating it without giving a practical application — the discovery of a principle alone is not an invention in patent-law sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the principle is applied to any special purpose producing a practical result, the patent may be good. The specification must apply the principle to matter organized to produce a practical result; otherwise it will be treated as claiming an unpatentable abstract principle (see Barrett v. Hall; Househill Co. v. Neilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a practical mode of carrying the principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the specification describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; the subject-matter becomes patentable when it is the mode of carrying the principle into effect rather than the principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a practical mode is described, on infringement the jury decides whether another mode is a colorable imitation of the patentee's mode. Examples where specification was sustained only when construed as claiming the specific machinery described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim all possible means of achieving the effect (overbroad universal claims are void)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that asserts the art of producing an effect by any means (e.g., 'to cut ice of a uniform size by means of an apparatus worked by any other power than human') is an overbroad claim to an abstract principle and is utterly void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must identify practical means or specific apparatus; overbroad 'by any means' claims will be struck down (example: Wyeth v. Stone). Courts will construe to the specific machinery or mode actually described when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — courts will treat vague functional claims as specific machinery if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specification appears to claim a function in the abstract, courts will, if possible, construe the claim as limited to the particular machinery or combination specially described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: claims framed as 'communication of motion ... which is produced as follows' were sustained only as claims to the specific machinery so described; broad functional drafting would otherwise be void.
